requirement: The Habeas crate MUST provide a root `Symposium.toml` with a `[[skills]]` group whose `source.path` is `assets/skills`. It MUST disable default skill groups so its bundled skills are selected from one source. It MUST declare a named `habeas` Cargo installation with `executable = "habeas"` and `global = true`, so `cargo agents use habeas` can provide the CLI globally.
rationale: The crate-root manifest selects assets/skills once and declares a named global Cargo installation for the habeas executable.

text: description: Design and vet requirements for new features or user-visible behavior changes in a Habeas mdBook project before coding; also maintain requirements and references.

When a user requests new or changed user-visible behavior in a Habeas project, first read the relevant requirements, code, and tests. Identify requirements that already express the intended behavior. For gaps, draft the smallest set of observable obligations, including important outcomes and failure cases, without committing to an implementation.

Show the user the full IDs and text of existing requirements to reuse, plus the proposed chapter location, full IDs, and exact fenced text of any additions or changes. State open product choices separately. Ask the user to agree to or revise this requirement set. User-provided exact requirement text or explicit agreement earlier in the conversation counts as approval; a general request to build the feature does not. Keep drafts out of the mdBook while review is pending, and do not write implementation or test code yet.

After agreement, install the approved requirements in the mdBook and confirm their names. Then implement the behavior, add tests and traceability references, and maintain evidence. If implementation reveals a substantive change to an approved obligation, review and install the revised requirement before coding that change. Use the evidence skill for pending determinations while implementation is incomplete.

Put requirements in the book's Markdown source directory. Define each with a fenced `{req}` directive: the opening line is three or more colons followed by `{req} name`, and the closing line has at least as many colons. Derive the full name from the chapter path relative to that directory: remove `.md`, change `/` to `.`, and append the directive name. For nested chapters, omit a leading `reqs/` and a trailing `/index` or `/README`.
Pressing q MUST stop managed forwards.

Everything between the fences is the requirement body, including headings, examples, and diagrams. Use a longer outer colon fence when the body contains a nested colon directive. Use BCP 14 terms when stating obligations.
Use fully qualified names for implementation, citation, and test references. Place them on the relevant source or book line:
When a requirement changes, update its `evidence/<full-name>.json` record. Run the Cargo tests to see all Habeas validation findings.
description: Record and repair Habeas evidence for requirements, source references, and Cargo validation failures.

For each requirement, maintain `evidence/<full-name>.json` with exactly `requirement`, `determination`, `rationale`, and `inputs`. Copy the current Markdown between the `{req}` directive's opening and closing fences into `requirement`, excluding leading and trailing whitespace. Set `determination` to `true` only after checking the implementation; otherwise use `false` and explain the remaining work in `rationale`.

An approved requirement may be installed before its implementation exists. Record it with `determination: false` and a rationale describing the pending work; an empty `inputs` array is valid until there are lines to cite. Expect validation to fail during this interval. Once code and tests satisfy the approved requirement, inspect them, snapshot their exact lines, and only then change the determination to `true`. Review a substantive change to the approved obligation with the user before changing its requirement text.

Each input names a repository-relative `file`, a 1-based inclusive `line_start` and `line_end`, and a `text` array containing the exact current text of those lines. Cite the lines that support the determination. Every `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference to the requirement must fall within one of its input ranges.

Run `cargo test --workspace` after changing requirements, source references, or evidence. Read the full set of Habeas errors: missing and orphan records, malformed fields, false determinations, stale requirement text, changed input lines, unknown references, and uncovered reference lines.
Do not make a failing check green by inventing input text or changing a determination without examining the cited files.
description: Build an initial Habeas requirement set from an existing codebase by tracing its tests and user-visible behavior; use for requirements bootstrapping or coverage audits.

Read the project's existing requirements, documentation, public entry points, implementation, and tests before writing new requirements. Follow behavior through the code rather than relying only on test names or top-level dispatch.
- Every first-party runnable test or test case, including integration tests, doctests, and parameterized cases where present. Record the requirement IDs each test checks.

- Every first-party source unit that appears to implement end-user-visible functionality or interactions. Record file locations and requirement IDs for relevant public APIs, commands, handlers, UI actions, configuration, outputs, errors, and distinct observable branches. Do not count one tagged entry point as coverage for deeper user-visible code.
Exclude generated and third-party code from the inventories. If a candidate looks user-facing but its purpose is unclear, keep it on the gap list until resolved.

Treat requirements inferred from existing code as proposals. Show the user their proposed full IDs and exact text, along with uncertainty about whether observed behavior is intended or a bug. Obtain agreement on the proposals before installing them in the mdBook; prior explicit agreement to the same requirements counts.

Create or reuse the agreed, stable, chapter-qualified `{req}` requirements in the mdBook. State observable obligations with BCP 14 terms. Group tests that check the same behavior under one requirement; several tests MAY share an ID. For tests of internal invariants, write a requirement for the invariant they actually check rather than inventing a user-facing promise. Distinguish intended behavior from a possible bug or incidental implementation detail.

Put at least one `{test}` reference with a full requirement name on each test definition or individual case. A parameterized test can carry a reference at its case source or generating declaration when that is the only editable source. Add multiple references when a test checks multiple requirements. Do not use one file-level tag to stand in for unrelated tests.

Map each inventoried user-visible source unit to a requirement and add `{impl}` references at meaningful implementation points, including distinct observable branches. Do not tag every line. Use the bundled `habeas-requirements` and `habeas-evidence` guidance for directive syntax and evidence records. Each evidence record must cite exact current lines covering every reference to its requirement. Judge the requirement from the code and test results; a tag alone does not justify `determination: true`.
For example, source comments can carry these references:

Run the project tests and Habeas validation, then review both inventories independently: Habeas checks references that exist but does not detect an untagged test or omitted user-visible code. Report test-tag coverage and user-visible implementation coverage as mapped counts over total counts. Claim 100% only when both inventories have no unmapped items. List remaining gaps with file locations and reasons; do not invent evidence or silently exclude difficult cases.
